question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If you heat a metal rod at one end (a)/ heat travels along its length (b)/ until the other end had become warm too (c)/ due to the process of conduction. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a zero conditional sentence expressing a general scientific truth, both the if-clause and the main clause must use the simple present tense. Since "travels" is present tense, "had become" must also be present tense: "becomes".

◦ Corrected sentence: If you heat a metal rod at one end, heat travels along its length until the other end becomes warm too, due to the process of conduction.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If you heat a metal rod at one end" is proper, in the simple present.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "heat travels along its length" is proper, in the simple present.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "due to the process of conduction" correctly completes the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• If you drop a stone in water, it had sunk. → it sinks (zero conditional: present simple + present simple, for general truths).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

If you notice any signs of a gas leak in the building, ___ the maintenance office immediately and evacuate the area.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. notify.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a zero conditional instruction sentence (if + present simple, ...imperative), the main clause must use the base form of the verb, since it is a command, not a statement. So the correct answer is "notify".

◦ Complete sentence: If you notice any signs of a gas leak in the building, notify the maintenance office immediately and evacuate the area.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "notified" — the simple past cannot serve as an imperative verb.

 

• Option 3: "will notify" — a plain instruction does not take "will"; the base form alone is used as a command.

 

• Option 4: "notifying" — a gerund or participle cannot serve as the main verb of an imperative sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• If the alarm rings, will leave the building at once. → leave the building at once (zero conditional with an imperative main clause uses the base verb).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If the negotiations fail to reach a consensus by Friday (a)/ the labour union will call (b)/ for an indefinite strike (c)/ that affected the entire supply chain. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a first conditional sentence, every verb in the main clause describing the future result must be in the simple future. Since "will call" is future, "affected" must also be "will affect".

◦ Corrected sentence: If the negotiations fail to reach a consensus by Friday, the labour union will call for an indefinite strike that will affect the entire supply chain.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If the negotiations fail to reach a consensus by Friday" is proper, in the simple present.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the labour union will call" is proper, in the simple future.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "for an indefinite strike" is a proper object phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• If the demand rises, the price increases and affected consumers badly. → and will affect consumers badly (every main-clause verb in a first conditional needs "will").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

If the fever persists beyond three days, the doctor ___ additional blood tests to rule out any infection.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. may recommend.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a first conditional sentence, the main clause may use a modal such as "may/can/must" instead of "will", to express possibility, ability, or obligation, but the verb must remain in the base form after the modal. So the correct answer is "may recommend".

◦ Complete sentence: If the fever persists beyond three days, the doctor may recommend additional blood tests to rule out any infection.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "recommended" — the simple past cannot express a future possibility in a first-conditional main clause.

 

• Option 3: "recommending" — a gerund cannot serve as the main verb of the clause.

 

• Option 4: "had recommended" — the past perfect is incompatible with a first-conditional main clause describing a future possibility.

 

NOTE

 

• If you break the rules, you must face the consequences., If the traffic clears, we can reach on time. (first-conditional main clause modals: may/can/must + base verb).

question:
Select the option that correctly transforms the given sentence into its formal inverted form (without "if").

 

If you should require any further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact our helpdesk.
option_1: Should you required any further assistance
option_2: If should you require any further assistance
option_3: Should you require any further assistance
option_4: Requiring should you any further assistance
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Should you require any further assistance.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A formal first conditional if-clause containing "should" can be inverted by dropping "if" and placing "should" before the subject, keeping the verb in the base form. So "If you should require" transforms into "Should you require".

◦ Transformed sentence: Should you require any further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact our helpdesk.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Should you required any further assistance" — the verb after the inverted "should" must be in the base form, not the past tense.

 

• Option 2: "If should you require any further assistance" — "if" and the inverted "should" construction cannot be combined; one replaces the other.

 

• Option 4: "Requiring should you any further assistance" — this word order is not a valid inversion pattern at all.

 

NOTE

 

• If you should need anything else, call this number. → Should you need anything else (formal first-conditional inversion drops "if" and fronts "should").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If the museum was open on public holidays (a)/ more tourists would visit (b)/ the ancient sculptures displayed (c)/ in the east wing. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a second conditional sentence, the verb "to be" in the if-clause is always "were", regardless of the subject. So "was" must be "were".

◦ Corrected sentence: If the museum were open on public holidays, more tourists would visit the ancient sculptures displayed in the east wing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "more tourists would visit" is proper, in the second-conditional main clause.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the ancient sculptures displayed" is a proper object phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "in the east wing" correctly completes the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• If the shop was closed on Sundays, sales would drop. → If the shop were closed (second conditional "to be" is always "were").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If the committee reconsidered the proposal seriously (a)/ it might approve (b)/ the additional budget (c)/ and would have released the funds within a week. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a second conditional sentence, every verb in the main clause must use "would/might/could" + base verb, not "would have + past participle". Since "might approve" is used, "would have released" must also be "would release".

◦ Corrected sentence: If the committee reconsidered the proposal seriously, it might approve the additional budget and would release the funds within a week.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If the committee reconsidered the proposal seriously" is proper, in the simple past.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "it might approve" is proper, using "might + base verb".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the additional budget" is a proper object phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• If he tried harder, he could succeed and would have impressed his mentor. → and would impress his mentor (every verb in a second-conditional main clause needs "would/might/could + base", not "would have").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Were the interest rates falls further next quarter, (a)/ home loan borrowers across the country would benefit significantly (b)/ from lower monthly instalments. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the formal inverted second conditional "Were + subject..." (equivalent to "If the interest rates were to fall..."), the verb after the subject must be in the infinitive form "to fall", not "falls". So "Were the interest rates falls" must be "Were the interest rates to fall".

◦ Corrected sentence: Were the interest rates to fall further next quarter, home loan borrowers across the country would benefit significantly from lower monthly instalments.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "home loan borrowers across the country would benefit significantly" is proper, using "would + base verb".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "from lower monthly instalments" correctly completes the sentence.

 

• Option (d) No error — this is incorrect since an error exists in part (a).

 

NOTE

 

• Were the government to lower taxes, spending would rise., Were she to apologise, he would forgive her. (inverted second conditional: "Were + subject + to + base verb").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If the shipment had cleared customs a day earlier (a)/ the retailer would restock (b)/ its shelves before the festival rush (c)/ instead of losing crucial sales. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a third conditional sentence (if + past perfect, ...would have + past participle), the main clause must use "would have" + past participle. So "would restock" must be "would have restocked".

◦ Corrected sentence: If the shipment had cleared customs a day earlier, the retailer would have restocked its shelves before the festival rush instead of losing crucial sales.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If the shipment had cleared customs a day earlier" is proper, in the past perfect.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "its shelves before the festival rush" is a proper object phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "instead of losing crucial sales" correctly completes the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• If she had left earlier, she would catch the train. → she would have caught (third conditional main clause needs "would have + past participle").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Had the referee reviewed the contentious decision on camera, (a)/ the outcome of the match (b)/ might be entirely different (c)/ from what the fans witnessed that evening. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Had the referee reviewed..." is an inverted third-conditional if-clause (equivalent to "If the referee had reviewed..."), so the main clause must use "might/would/could have" + past participle. So "might be" must be "might have been".

◦ Corrected sentence: Had the referee reviewed the contentious decision on camera, the outcome of the match might have been entirely different from what the fans witnessed that evening.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Had the referee reviewed the contentious decision on camera," is a proper inverted third-conditional if-clause.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the outcome of the match" is a proper subject phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "from what the fans witnessed that evening" correctly completes the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• Had she left on time, she might catch the earlier train. → she might have caught (an inverted third-conditional main clause needs "might/would/could have + past participle").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

If the antique vase had been packed more carefully by the movers, (a)/ it would not shattered during transit (b)/ to the new gallery. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a third conditional main clause, the verb must be "would have" + past participle. So "would not shattered" must be "would not have shattered".

◦ Corrected sentence: If the antique vase had been packed more carefully by the movers, it would not have shattered during transit to the new gallery.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If the antique vase had been packed more carefully by the movers," is a proper passive past-perfect if-clause.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to the new gallery" correctly completes the sentence.

 

• Option (d) No error — this is incorrect since an error exists in part (b).

 

NOTE

 

• If he had listened, he would not lost his job. → he would not have lost (third conditional main clause needs "would have + past participle").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If the negotiators had reached an agreement last year (a)/ the two neighbouring countries (b)/ would have enjoyed uninterrupted trade relations (c)/ at this very moment. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This is a mixed conditional: the if-clause refers to a past condition ("had reached"), but the result described is in the present (signalled by "at this very moment"). So the main clause must use "would + base verb" (or "would be + -ing"), not "would have + past participle": "would have enjoyed" must be "would be enjoying".

◦ Corrected sentence: If the negotiators had reached an agreement last year, the two neighbouring countries would be enjoying uninterrupted trade relations at this very moment.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If the negotiators had reached an agreement last year" is a proper past-perfect if-clause.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the two neighbouring countries" is a proper subject phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "at this very moment" correctly signals a present-time result.

 

NOTE

 

• If I had saved more money, I would have travelled the world right now. → I would be travelling the world right now (a past condition with a present-time result needs "would + base / would be + -ing", not "would have").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If he were the kind of manager who reviews every detail personally (a)/ he will have caught (b)/ the invoicing error (c)/ that slipped through last month's audit. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This is a mixed conditional: the if-clause describes a general, present-time character trait ("were the kind of manager who..."), but the result is a specific past event ("last month's audit"). Such a result still needs "would have" + past participle, not "will have". So "will have caught" must be "would have caught".

◦ Corrected sentence: If he were the kind of manager who reviews every detail personally, he would have caught the invoicing error that slipped through last month's audit.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If he were the kind of manager who reviews every detail personally" is a proper present-tense if-clause describing a general trait.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the invoicing error" is a proper object phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "that slipped through last month's audit" correctly signals a specific past-time result.

 

NOTE

 

• If she were more careful by nature, she would have avoided that mistake last week., If he were punctual as a rule, he would have caught yesterday's early train. (a general present trait with a specific past result still needs "would have + past participle").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

___ the shareholders approve the merger unanimously, the deal will not proceed to the next stage.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Unless.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Unless" means "if...not". Since the main clause already states a negative consequence ("will not proceed"), the condition must be framed as "if the shareholders do not approve", which is exactly what "Unless" expresses.

◦ Complete sentence: Unless the shareholders approve the merger unanimously, the deal will not proceed to the next stage.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "If" — using plain "if" here would require the main clause to be rephrased as "...will not proceed" only if the approval does NOT happen, which "if" alone does not convey.

 

• Option 2: "Provided" — "provided" introduces a condition that ensures a positive outcome, which does not fit here without the word "that" and reverses the intended logic.

 

• Option 3: "Although" — "although" introduces a contrast, not a condition, and does not fit this sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• Unless you apologise, she will not forgive you., Unless it rains, the match will go ahead. ("unless" = "if...not").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The bank will sanction the education loan ___ the applicant furnishes a valid co-signatory and proof of admission.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. provided that.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Provided that / providing (that) / on condition that" functions as "if", introducing a necessary condition that must be satisfied for the main clause to hold true. So the correct answer is "provided that".

◦ Complete sentence: The bank will sanction the education loan provided that the applicant furnishes a valid co-signatory and proof of admission.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "unless" — this would mean the loan is sanctioned only if the applicant does NOT furnish the documents, which reverses the intended meaning.

 

• Option 3: "even if" — this would suggest the loan is sanctioned regardless of whether the documents are furnished, which is incorrect.

 

• Option 4: "in case" — this would suggest the documents are furnished as a precaution, not as a necessary condition for sanction.

 

NOTE

 

• You may leave early, provided that you finish your assigned tasks., The trek will proceed, on condition that the weather stays clear. ("provided that / on condition that" = "if").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

You may continue to use the company laptop after resignation ___ you return it within thirty days of your last working day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. as long as.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "As long as / so long as" means "if", introducing a condition that must remain true for the duration of the main clause's validity. So the correct answer is "as long as".

◦ Complete sentence: You may continue to use the company laptop after resignation as long as you return it within thirty days of your last working day.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "even if" — this would suggest permission is granted regardless of whether the laptop is returned, which reverses the intended meaning.

 

• Option 2: "in case" — this would suggest the return is a precaution rather than the actual condition for continued use.

 

• Option 3: "unless" — this would mean permission is granted only if the laptop is NOT returned, which reverses the intended meaning.

 

NOTE

 

• You can borrow my car, as long as you refill the fuel tank., The offer stays valid, so long as you register before Friday. ("as long as / so long as" = "if", for a condition lasting throughout).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

___ the results are declared today, the official merit list will still not be published before next week, since further scrutiny is mandatory regardless of the declaration date.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Even if.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Even if" introduces a condition that does not change the outcome — here, the sentence explicitly states that the delay happens "regardless of the declaration date", so the merit list stays delayed whether or not the results are declared today. This contrasts with "unless", which would wrongly suggest that declaring the results today could actually bring the list out sooner.

◦ Complete sentence: Even if the results are declared today, the official merit list will still not be published before next week, since further scrutiny is mandatory regardless of the declaration date.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Unless" — this would mean the list is delayed only if the results are NOT declared today, which is not the intended meaning.

 

• Option 2: "Provided that" — this would suggest declaring the results today is a necessary condition for the list, which contradicts the sentence.

 

• Option 4: "As long as" — this would suggest the delay lasts only while the results remain undeclared, which does not fit.

 

NOTE

 

• Even if it rains heavily, the outdoor event will continue as scheduled., Even if he apologises, she will not forgive him easily. ("even if" = a condition that does not affect the stated outcome).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Keep a printed copy of your admit card ___ the online verification system fails on the day of the examination.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. in case.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "In case" introduces a precaution taken in advance to prepare for a possible future event, unlike "if", which introduces a direct condition-result relationship. Since keeping a printed copy is a precaution against a possible system failure, the correct answer is "in case".

◦ Complete sentence: Keep a printed copy of your admit card in case the online verification system fails on the day of the examination.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "if" — "if" would suggest the printed copy is needed only as a direct response once the system actually fails, not as an advance precaution.

 

• Option 3: "unless" — this would reverse the intended meaning, suggesting the copy is needed only when the system does NOT fail.

 

• Option 4: "provided that" — this would wrongly frame the system failing as a necessary condition for keeping the copy.

 

NOTE

 

• Carry an umbrella in case it rains later., Keep some cash handy in case the card machine stops working. ("in case" = a precaution against a possible future event).

question:
Select the option that correctly transforms the given sentence using the concise "But for" construction.

 

If it had not been for the quick thinking of the bystanders, the accident victim would not have survived.
option_1: Unless for the quick thinking of the bystanders
option_2: Except for that the quick thinking of the bystanders
option_3: Without for the quick thinking of the bystanders
option_4: But for the quick thinking of the bystanders
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. But for the quick thinking of the bystanders.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "But for" followed directly by a noun phrase is a concise, formal equivalent of "If it had not been for" followed by a noun phrase, used to introduce a hypothetical negative condition.

◦ Transformed sentence: But for the quick thinking of the bystanders, the accident victim would not have survived.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Unless for the quick thinking of the bystanders" — "unless" is followed by a clause, not directly by a noun phrase in this construction, so "unless for" is not standard usage.

 

• Option 2: "Except for that the quick thinking of the bystanders" — this is not a recognised way of forming a hypothetical negative condition before a main clause.

 

• Option 3: "Without for the quick thinking of the bystanders" — "without for" is not standard usage; "without" is not combined with "for" in this construction.

 

NOTE

 

• If it had not been for her timely warning, we would have missed the deadline. → But for her timely warning ("but for" + noun phrase = "if it had not been for" + noun phrase).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

___ you lost your passport while travelling abroad, what would be your first course of action?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Supposing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Suppose / Supposing (that)" functions as a conditional conjunction meaning "if", typically introducing a hypothetical scenario for discussion. So the correct answer is "Supposing".

◦ Complete sentence: Supposing you lost your passport while travelling abroad, what would be your first course of action?

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Because" — this introduces a reason, not a hypothetical condition, and does not fit the sentence.

 

• Option 2: "Whereas" — this introduces a contrast between two facts, not a hypothetical scenario.

 

• Option 3: "Despite" — this introduces a concession, not a condition, and cannot begin a clause of this type.

 

NOTE

 

• Suppose you won the lottery tomorrow, what would you do first?, Supposing the flight gets delayed, shall we wait or reschedule? ("suppose / supposing that" = "if", introducing a hypothetical scenario).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If only I had invested in that start-up (a)/ when my colleague first suggested it, (b)/ I am a millionaire today (c)/ instead of regretting my hesitation. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "If only" expressing a past regret with a present consequence works like a mixed conditional: the subordinate clause uses the past perfect ("had invested"), but the main clause describing the present result must use "would be" + base verb, not the simple present. So "I am" must be "I would be".

◦ Corrected sentence: If only I had invested in that start-up when my colleague first suggested it, I would be a millionaire today instead of regretting my hesitation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If only I had invested in that start-up" is a proper past-perfect clause of regret.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "when my colleague first suggested it," is a proper adverbial clause, in the simple past.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "instead of regretting my hesitation" correctly completes the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• If only she had studied medicine, she is a doctor by now. → she would be a doctor by now ("if only" + past perfect, with a present result, needs "would be + base verb").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The manager speaks about the failed project (a)/ so casually (b)/ as if it don't matter at all (c)/ to the company's reputation. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "as if / as though" expressing an unreal comparison, an ordinary verb (other than "to be") takes the simple past subjunctive form. So "it don't matter" must be "it didn't matter".

◦ Corrected sentence: The manager speaks about the failed project so casually as if it didn't matter at all to the company's reputation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The manager speaks about the failed project" is proper, in the simple present.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "so casually" is a proper adverbial phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "to the company's reputation" correctly completes the comparison.

 

NOTE

 

• He orders people around as if he own the company. → as if he owned the company ("as if / as though" + simple past, for an unreal comparison with an ordinary verb).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The old sailor described the storm so vividly, (a)/ as if he has personally witnessed it decades ago, (b)/ when he was still a young cadet. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "as if / as though", when the comparison refers to a time earlier than the main verb, the subordinate clause must use the past perfect. So "has personally witnessed" must be "had personally witnessed".

◦ Corrected sentence: The old sailor described the storm so vividly, as if he had personally witnessed it decades ago, when he was still a young cadet.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The old sailor described the storm so vividly," is proper, in the simple past.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "when he was still a young cadet" is a proper adverbial clause, in the simple past.

 

• Option (d) No error — this is incorrect since an error exists in part (b).

 

NOTE

 

• She talked about the film as if she has already seen it years before. → as if she had already seen it ("as if / as though" + past perfect, for an unreal comparison referring to an earlier time).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

I wish my neighbours turn down (a)/ their music late at night (b)/ since it disturbs my sleep (c)/ almost every day. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "I wish" expressing annoyance or a complaint about someone else's persistent behaviour requires "would" in the subordinate clause, not the simple present. So "turn down" must be "would turn down".

◦ Corrected sentence: I wish my neighbours would turn down their music late at night since it disturbs my sleep almost every day.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "their music late at night" is a proper object phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "since it disturbs my sleep" is a proper reason clause.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "almost every day" correctly completes the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• I wish he stops interrupting me during meetings. → I wish he would stop interrupting me ("I wish" + "would", for a complaint about someone else's repeated behaviour).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If the airline had not cancelled the connecting flight (a)/ and if the weather conditions had remained favourable throughout the journey, (b)/ the passengers will reach (c)/ their destination without any inconvenience. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This sentence has two if-clauses, both in the past perfect ("had not cancelled", "had remained"), forming a third conditional. The main clause must therefore use "would have" + past participle. So "will reach" must be "would have reached".

◦ Corrected sentence: If the airline had not cancelled the connecting flight and if the weather conditions had remained favourable throughout the journey, the passengers would have reached their destination without any inconvenience.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If the airline had not cancelled the connecting flight" is a proper past-perfect if-clause.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "and if the weather conditions had remained favourable throughout the journey," is a proper second past-perfect if-clause.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "their destination without any inconvenience" correctly completes the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• If he had studied harder and if he had managed his time well, he will pass with distinction. → he would have passed with distinction (two past-perfect if-clauses still require a third-conditional main clause, "would have + past participle").
